newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel budget chief says 1997 reserve is used up.
newsitem.headline: Israel budget chief says 1997 reserve is used up.

text.p: The Israeli government has already committed the entire 1997 budget reserve and any further spending increases will have to come out of the general budget, Treasury budget director Ron Croll said on Thursday.
"The commitments made on the general reserve budget are bigger than the reserve....It is (now) impossible to make budgetary decisions using the reserve," Croll told Reuters.
He rejected Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel's call for immediate measures to contain the budget deficit after the Treasury said the deficit reached 1.28 billion shekels in January.
"We still do not have enough data to implement a cut. It would be a mistake to cut now," Croll said.
The government's approximately 190 billion shekel budget is aimed at keeping the deficit to 2.8 percent of gross doemstic product.
Croll attributed the unusually high expenses in January to one-time advance payments to the Defence Ministry and the health system. "On the expense side, I don't see any problems in 1997," he added.
Revenues were under forecast for the month, but Croll said it was too early to see whether that represented a trend.

He warned that if the deficit looks to be exceeding the target - a trend he said would become evident as early as March -- the cabinet would have to cut spending more than the approximately seven billion shekels already undertaken.
"It would be a mistake to raise taxes in today's economy," he said.

Croll said the reserve had already been committed to 300 million shekels in higher defence spending, 400-500 million shekels for "coalition agreements" and subsidies to the health system. He estimated total commitments were 1.8-1.9 billion shekels, 300-400 million shekels more than the reserve.
On Tuesday, Finance Minister Dan Meridor said he would update ministers on the budget at the next weekly cabinet meeting, but Meridor said he planned no action on spending before April.
